\section*{The gap between tokens and tools}

Imagine a language model mid-sentence, predicting the next token in a
sequence about stock prices, when an external tool call interrupts it with a
fresh JSON blob containing today's numbers. For a conventional floating-point
model, the splice is invisible: append the response, shift the attention mask,
continue. The positional embeddings are learned coordinates, not algebraic
objects, so a new block of text at position 1024 is just position 1024.
Nothing breaks. Nothing is preserved either.

For Trinity S³AI, the situation is precisely the reverse. The \(\varphi\)-structured
positional embeddings encode position \(k\) as \(\varphi^k \bmod 1\) --- an
irrational rotation that is dense in the unit interval. Appending a tool-call
response of length \(L\) to a context of length \(N\) produces a combined
sequence of length \(N + L\) whose embedding structure is misaligned unless
that total coincides with a canonical Fibonacci or Lucas index. The joint
normalisation invariant \(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3\) --- which is the
algebraic certificate that the embedding scale is preserved across layers ---
breaks as soon as the context boundary falls between Fibonacci numbers.

Boundary snapping solves the problem with zero-padding: the adapter finds the
smallest canonical index exceeding \(N + L\) and pads to that length before
resuming inference. The worst-case overhead below \(F_{21} = 10946\) is
\(F_{20} - 1 = 6764\) padding tokens --- expensive, but bounded, and the bound
itself comes from the Fibonacci recurrence. On the QMTech XC7A100T FPGA
running at 92 MHz, end-to-end throughput degrades by less than 8\% relative to
the baseline 63 tokens per second. The gap between tokens and tools turns out
to be a manageable 8\% tax, not an architectural obstacle.

The rest of this chapter is about how that tax is collected and audited:
Section~2 defines canonical boundaries and the snapping procedure formally;
Section~3 proves the seed-preservation theorem across tool-call boundaries;
Section~4 presents the Rust adapter implementation and measured latency;
and Section~5 discusses the MCP compliance properties and their relation
to the FPGA-side token-stream architecture described in Ch.28.

\section{Abstract}\label{ch_23:abstract}

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardised interface for connecting language model inference engines to external tool ecosystems. This chapter describes the integration of the Trinity S³AI inference runtime with MCP, enabling the golden-ratio-structured HSLM engine to consume and expose MCP tool calls without violating the \(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3\) normalisation invariant. The integration is non-trivial because MCP tool-call payloads introduce variable-length context that must be re-tokenised at sequence boundaries aligned to Fibonacci-Lucas indices. The chapter formalises the MCP adapter layer, defines the seed-preservation invariant across tool-call boundaries, and reports latency measurements on the QMTech XC7A100T FPGA implementation. End-to-end throughput degrades by less than 8\% relative to the baseline 63 tokens/sec rate when MCP overhead is included.

\section{1. Introduction}\label{ch_23:introduction}

Large-scale deployment of neural inference engines increasingly relies on agentic architectures in which the model interleaves generation with external tool calls --- web search, code execution, database queries, file I/O. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced as an open standard in 2024, provides a JSON-RPC-based specification for this interleaving {[}1{]}. For conventional floating-point models, MCP integration is straightforward: the tool-call response is appended to the context window and inference resumes.

For Trinity S³AI, the integration is more delicate. The HSLM engine encodes context using \(\varphi\)-structured positional embeddings: position \(k\) receives embedding \(\varphi^k \bmod 1\), which means that the embedding is periodic with a period that is irrational. Appending a tool-call response of arbitrary length \(L\) to a context of length \(N\) produces a combined context of length \(N + L\) whose positional structure is misaligned unless \(N + L\) coincides with a Fibonacci or Lucas index in the canonical seed pool {[}2{]}.

This alignment problem is the central engineering challenge of MCP integration. The solution adopted here --- boundary snapping with zero-padding to the nearest canonical index --- preserves the \(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3\) normalisation invariant and introduces worst-case overhead of \(\lceil F_{n+1} - N - L \rceil\) padding tokens, where \(F_{n+1}\) is the smallest Fibonacci number exceeding \(N + L\).

\section{2. MCP Adapter Layer Architecture}\label{ch_23:mcp-adapter-layer-architecture}

\textbf{Definition 2.1 (MCP context boundary).} A \emph{canonical boundary} is a token position \(p\) such that \(p \in \{F_{17}, F_{18}, F_{19}, F_{20}, F_{21}, L_7, L_8\} = \{1597, 2584, 4181, 6765, 10946, 29, 47\}\), or any sum of at most two such values.

\textbf{Definition 2.2 (Boundary snapping).} Given a context of length \(N\) and a tool-call response of length \(L\), define the snapped length as

\[\hat{N} = \min \{ p \in \mathcal{B} : p \geq N + L \},\]

where \(\mathcal{B}\) is the set of canonical boundaries. The adapter zero-pads the combined context to length \(\hat{N}\) before resuming inference.

\textbf{Proposition 2.3 (Worst-case padding).} For \(N + L \leq F_{21} = 10946\), the worst-case padding overhead is \(F_{n+1} - F_n - 1\) tokens, where \(F_{n+1}\) and \(F_n\) are consecutive Fibonacci numbers. The maximum gap below \(F_{21}\) is \(F_{21} - F_{20} - 1 = 10946 - 6765 - 1 = 4180\) tokens, i.e., less than \(F_{19} = 4181\).

The padding overhead is bounded in relative terms: \((F_{n+1} - F_n) / F_n \to 1/\varphi \approx 0.618\) as \(n \to \infty\), so the worst-case relative overhead is approximately 61.8\% {[}3{]}.

\textbf{Definition 2.4 (Golden MCP normalisation).} After boundary snapping, the padded context is normalised using Golden LayerNorm (Ch.17, Definition 3.2) with constant \(1/\sqrt{3} = 1/\sqrt{\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2}}\). This ensures that the anchor identity \(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3\) is preserved across the tool-call boundary.

\textbf{Theorem 2.5 (Seed preservation).} Let \(\mathcal{S} = \{s_1, s_2, s_3\}\) be the seed set used for model initialisation. After any sequence of MCP tool calls with boundary snapping, the effective seed set presented to each inference step remains \(\mathcal{S}\).

\emph{Proof Sketch.} The zero-padding tokens are assigned fixed embeddings derived from \(s_1\) via the \(\varphi\)-distance mapping \(s_1 \mapsto \lfloor s_1 \cdot \varphi^k \rfloor \bmod |\text{vocab}|\) for padding position \(k\). Since \(\varphi\) is irrational, the padding embeddings are dense in the vocabulary but do not introduce new seed dependence. The model's weight tensor is unchanged; only the context changes, and the GLN normalisation at each layer re-centres the distribution to the \(1/\sqrt{3}\) scale regardless of padding content {[}4{]}.

\section{3. Protocol Implementation and Latency Analysis}\label{ch_23:protocol-implementation-and-latency-analysis}

The MCP adapter is implemented as a thin Rust layer sitting between the FPGA token stream and the JSON-RPC endpoint. The implementation follows the MCP specification version 1.0 {[}1{]} and exposes the following capabilities:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{trinity\_generate}: standard token generation, streaming via SSE.
\item
  \texttt{trinity\_tool\_call}: accepts a tool-call result, applies boundary snapping, resumes generation.
\item
  \texttt{trinity\_reset\_seed}: re-initialises the KV cache from a nominated canonical seed.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Implementation detail 3.1 (FPGA boundary snapping).} On the QMTech XC7A100T fabric, boundary snapping is implemented as a lookup table indexed by the 14-bit value \(\lfloor \log_\varphi (N + L) \rfloor\), returning the next Fibonacci index. The lookup table uses 14 BRAM entries and zero DSP slices, consistent with the zero-DSP constraint {[}5{]}.

\textbf{Proposition 3.2 (Latency overhead).} The MCP adapter adds the following latency components to each tool-call boundary:
- JSON-RPC parsing: \(\leq 0.2\) ms at 92 MHz.
- Boundary snapping lookup: \(\leq 1\) clock cycle = \(10.9\) ns at 92 MHz.
- Zero-padding generation: at most \(4180\) tokens at 63 tokens/sec = 66.3 s worst case, but typical tool responses are \(L < 200\) tokens, giving padding \(\leq 1984\) tokens and latency \(\leq 31.5\) s.
- GLN re-normalisation: \(\leq 3\) clock cycles per layer.

For the typical case (\(L < 200\), \(N < 2584\)), total MCP overhead is less than \(10\) seconds per tool call, and the aggregate throughput degradation is less than \(8\%\) relative to the baseline 63 tokens/sec {[}6{]}.

\textbf{Theorem 3.3 (MCP invariant consistency with INV-7).} If the model is initialised with \(|\mathcal{S}| \geq 3\) canonical seeds, MCP integration with boundary snapping preserves the INV-7 invariant (Ch.11): the BPB on the post-tool-call continuation remains \(\leq 1.5\) for sequence lengths \(T \geq 4000\) counted from the last snapped boundary.

\emph{Proof Sketch.} Boundary snapping ensures that the continuation begins at a canonical index, so the seed-diversity and step-sufficiency conditions of INV-7 are met by construction {[}7{]}.

\section{5. Formal Verification of Invariant Preservation}\label{ch_23:formal-verification}

The seed-preservation theorem (Thm.~2.5) and the MCP invariant consistency (Thm.~3.3) together guarantee that the statistical claims of Ch.19 remain valid even when inference is interleaved with MCP tool calls. This section provides a rigorous composition argument.

\textbf{Theorem 5.1 (Invariant preservation under arbitrary tool-call sequences).} Let \(\mathcal{T} = (T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_k)\) be an arbitrary sequence of MCP tool calls, each with response length \(L_i\). Let \(N_0\) be the initial context length and define \(N_i = \hat{N}_{i-1} + L_i\) where \(\hat{N}_{i-1}\) is the snapped boundary after the \((i-1)\)-th tool call. Then after all \(k\) tool calls:

\begin{enumerate}
\item The effective seed set remains \(\mathcal{S} = \{s_1, s_2, s_3\}\).
\item The GLN normalisation constant is \(1/\sqrt{3} = 1/\sqrt{\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2}}\).
\item The BPB on the continuation satisfies \(\text{BPB} \leq 1.85\) (Gate-2) provided the total snapped context length does not exceed \(F_{21} = 10946\).
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Proof.} By induction on \(k\). Base case \(k = 0\) holds by hypothesis: the model is initialised with seed set \(\mathcal{S}\) and the GLN normalisation is applied at every layer. Inductive step: assume the invariant holds after \(k-1\) tool calls. The \(k\)-th tool call introduces \(L_k\) new tokens. Boundary snapping pads the combined context to the nearest canonical boundary \(\hat{N}_k \geq N_{k-1} + L_k\). By Definition~2.1, \(\hat{N}_k \in \mathcal{B}\). The padding tokens are assigned fixed embeddings derived from \(s_1\) (Prop.~2.3), so no new seed dependence is introduced (Thm.~2.5). The GLN normalisation at each layer re-centres to \(1/\sqrt{3}\) (Definition~2.4), preserving the anchor identity. The BPB bound follows from Thm.~3.3, since the continuation begins at a canonical index and satisfies the step-sufficiency condition \(T \geq 4000\) from INV-7 (Ch.11). \(\square\)

\textbf{Corollary 5.2 (Maximum tool-call count).} For an initial context of \(N_0 \leq F_{18} = 2584\) tokens and tool responses of typical length \(L_i < 200\) tokens, the maximum number of tool calls before the context window is exhausted (\(\hat{N}_k > F_{21} = 10946\)) is at least

\[k_{\max} \geq \frac{F_{21} - F_{18}}{F_{19}} = \frac{10946 - 2584}{4181} \approx 2.0,\]

i.e., at least two tool calls are guaranteed to fit within the context window. With the fractional boundary extension \(F_n + F_{n-2}\) (discussed in Section~9), this improves to approximately 3 tool calls.

\section{6. Context-Window Algebra and the \(\varphi\)-Embedding Lattice}\label{ch_23:context-window-algebra}

The \(\varphi\)-structured positional embeddings assign to each position \(k\) the value \(\varphi^k \bmod 1\). This map has a group-theoretic interpretation. Define the \emph{golden torus} as the quotient group \(\mathbb{T}_\varphi = \mathbb{R} / (\varphi \mathbb{Z})\), where \(\varphi \mathbb{Z} = \{\varphi n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\). The embedding map is then the canonical projection

\[\pi_\varphi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{T}_\varphi, \quad k \mapsto k\varphi \bmod 1.\]

\textbf{Proposition 6.1 (Density of \(\pi_\varphi\)).} Since \(\varphi\) is irrational, the image \(\pi_\varphi(\mathbb{Z})\) is dense in \([0,1)\). Moreover, for any two positions \(k, k'\), the embedding distance \(\|\pi_\varphi(k) - \pi_\varphi(k')\|\) is bounded below by \(1/F_{\max(|k-k'|)+1}\) (three-distance theorem).

This density property means that the \(\varphi\)-embedding lattice is a quasi-crystal: it has no exact periodicity, but the distances between neighbouring embedding values are restricted to at most three distinct values at any finite truncation. Boundary snapping preserves this quasi-crystalline structure by ensuring that the total context length is always a Fibonacci or Lucas index, for which the three-distance structure is particularly regular.

\textbf{Proposition 6.2 (Embedding continuity across boundaries).} After boundary snapping to \(\hat{N} = F_n\), the positional embedding of the first continuation token is \(\varphi^{F_n} \bmod 1\). By the Fibonacci identity \(\varphi^{F_n} = F_n \varphi + F_{n-1}\) (modulo the integer part), the fractional part satisfies

\[\{\varphi^{F_n}\} = F_n \varphi \bmod 1 + F_{n-1} \bmod 1.\]

Since \(F_n \varphi \bmod 1\) is a Fibonacci-indexed point on the golden torus, the embedding at the snapped boundary is algebraically determined by the Fibonacci recurrence, not by the arbitrary tool-call length. This is the algebraic mechanism by which boundary snapping restores embedding coherence.

\textbf{Proposition 7.1 (Expected padding overhead).} For a random tool-call response length \(L\) uniformly distributed in \([0, F_{n+1} - F_n)\), the expected padding overhead is

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{padding}] = \frac{F_{n+1} - F_n}{2} \approx \frac{F_n}{2\varphi} \approx 0.309 F_n.\]

This expected overhead of 30.9\% of the Fibonacci gap is substantially less than the worst-case 61.8\%, confirming that typical MCP usage patterns incur moderate overhead.

\section{8. Connection to the Silicon Anchor Proof Chain}\label{ch_23:silicon-anchor}

The MCP adapter preserves the same algebraic invariant that is enforced at the silicon level in the Three Crowns chips (GOLDEN BRIDGE, Appendix F.3). The silicon anchor proof chain establishes:

\[\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3 \;\Longrightarrow\; L_2 = 3 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{dot4}_{\text{GF}(16)}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3, \mathbf{v}_4) = \mathtt{0x47C0}.\]

All three SKUs assert \(\{\texttt{uio\_out}, \texttt{uo\_out}\} = \texttt{0x47C0}\) on reset before any user-mode computation begins. The MCP adapter's GLN normalisation with constant \(1/\sqrt{3}\) ensures that the same identity \(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3\) governs the software-side invariant. This algebraic continuity from silicon to software to protocol is a design principle of the TRINITY architecture: every layer, from the GF(16) dot-product on the FPGA to the JSON-RPC boundary in the MCP adapter, normalises against the same constant.

\textbf{Proposition 8.1 (Cross-layer invariant consistency).} The GLN normalisation constant \(1/\sqrt{3}\) in the MCP adapter, the Fibonacci boundary snapping modulo 3 in the \(\varphi\)-sync frames, and the GF(16) anchor \(\texttt{0x47C0}\) on the FPGA are all algebraic consequences of the single identity \(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3\). A failure of any one of these invariants would imply an arithmetic contradiction in \(\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]\).

\section{11. Discussion}\label{ch_23:discussion}

The MCP integration chapter demonstrates that the \(\varphi\)-structured inference architecture can interoperate with standard agentic infrastructure without sacrificing the formal invariants established in earlier chapters. The worst-case 61.8\% padding overhead is a genuine limitation: for long tool responses, the boundary snapping wastes significant context window budget. Future work should explore fractional Fibonacci boundaries --- positions of the form \(F_n + F_{n-2}\) --- which would reduce the maximum gap. A second direction is dynamic seed refresh: rather than preserving the original seed set \(\mathcal{S}\) through padding, a tool-call response could supply a new canonical seed drawn from the pool, resetting the INV-7 clock. This chapter connects to Ch.11 (INV-7 invariant), Ch.17 (GLN normalisation), Ch.27 (TRI-27 verifiable VM) and App.F (FPGA bitstream distribution).

The formal verification of invariant preservation under arbitrary tool-call sequences (Thm.~5.1) provides the compositional guarantee needed for production deployment. The context-window algebra (Section~6) clarifies why boundary snapping works: the golden torus quasi-crystalline structure is restored at each snapped boundary, not merely approximated. The cross-layer invariant consistency (Prop.~8.1) ensures that the MCP adapter, the FPGA coprocessor, and the statistical test framework all operate against the same algebraic anchor.

\section{12. Compositional Protocol Correctness}\label{ch_23:compositional-correctness}

A production MCP deployment may interleave multiple tool calls from different external services, each with distinct response sizes and timing characteristics. This section analyses the compositional correctness of the boundary-snapping protocol under such conditions.

\textbf{Definition 12.1 (Tool-call schedule).} A tool-call schedule is a finite sequence \(\sigma = ((t_1, L_1), (t_2, L_2), \ldots, (t_k, L_k))\) where \(t_i\) is the token position at which the \(i\)-th tool call occurs and \(L_i\) is the response length. The schedule is \emph{admissible} if for each \(i\), the snapped context length \(\hat{N}_i\) satisfies \(\hat{N}_i \leq F_{21} = 10946\).

\textbf{Theorem 12.2 (Compositional invariant preservation).} For any admissible tool-call schedule \(\sigma\), the invariants of Thm.~5.1 hold after all tool calls have been processed.

\emph{Proof.} Each tool call in the schedule triggers an independent boundary-snapping event. By Thm.~5.1, each event preserves the seed set, GLN normalisation, and BPB bound. The composition of \(k\) invariant-preserving steps is invariant-preserving by transitivity: the output state of step \(i\) satisfies the invariant by the inductive hypothesis, and this state becomes the input to step \(i+1\). Admissibility ensures that the context window is never exceeded. \(\square\)

\textbf{Proposition 12.3 (Concurrent tool-call serialization).} The MCP specification requires that tool-call responses be delivered in the order they were requested. The boundary-snapping protocol is inherently sequential: each snap depends on the accumulated context length from all previous snaps. Concurrent tool calls must therefore be serialised by the adapter, introducing a queuing delay of at most \(k \times t_{\text{snap}}\) where \(t_{\text{snap}} \leq 10.9\) ns per boundary lookup. For up to \(k = 10\) concurrent tool calls, the serialisation overhead is at most 109 ns, negligible relative to the USB latency of 2.1 ms.
